s: Say where you are first.
What happened and how many people are hurt.
Follow the dispatcher's instructions.
Do not hang up until told to.
Look for traffic, fire, fumes, electricity.
Protect yourself: you cannot help if you get hurt.
Wear gloves if you have them.
Then check the person and call {EMS}.
Gloves, gauze pads, bandages, adhesive tape.
Scissors, tweezers, cold pack, emergency blanket.
A tourniquet and a CPR face mask.
Emergency numbers: {EMS} and {POISON}.
Wear disposable gloves if you have them.
Use a CPR face mask for rescue breaths.
Remove gloves inside out, without touching the outside.
Wash your hands with soap and water afterward.
Park safely, hazard lights on.
Call {EMS} and say exactly where you are.
Turn off engines if you can do it safely.
Do not move the injured unless there is fire or danger.
Feet apart, close to the load.
Bend your knees, keep your back straight.
Lift with your legs, not your back.
Do not twist; turn your feet instead.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

s: Pull the pin.
Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire.
Squeeze the handle.
Sweep side to side. Not out in seconds: leave, call {EMS}.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain
FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

s: No flames, no switches, no phone calls inside.
Get everyone out and leave the door open.
Call the gas company or {EMS} from outside.
Shut the meter valve only if you know how.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

s: Two ways out of every room.
Smoke alarms on every level; test them monthly.
Pick a meeting place outside.
Practice with everyone twice a year.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

s: Stop where you are. Do not run.
Drop to the ground, cover your face with your hands.
Roll over and over until the flames are out.
Cool the burn with water for at least 10 minutes.

cards.w: Smoke fills a room in minutes
s: Get low and crawl under the smoke.
Touch doors with the back of your hand: hot means use another way.
Close doors behind you.
Get out, stay out, call {EMS} from outside.
Watch children in water at all times, within arm's reach.
Fence pools on all four sides.
Life jackets on boats and in open water.
Learn CPR: every second counts.
Drop to your hands and knees.
Cover your head and neck under a sturdy table.
Hold on until the shaking stops.
Do not run outside during the shaking.
Go to a basement or a small room on the lowest floor.
Stay away from windows.
Cover your head and neck.
In a mobile home or car: get to a sturdy building.

cards.w: Fast water is stronger than it looks
s: 6 in (15 cm) of moving water can knock you down.
1 ft (30 cm) can sweep a car away.
Never walk or drive through floodwater.
Go to higher ground and call {EMS} if trapped.
Hear thunder? You are close enough to be struck.
Get inside a building or a hard-top car.
Avoid open fields, hilltops, water and lone trees.
Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
Never run a generator indoors or in a garage.
Keep it at least 20 ft (6 m) from doors and windows.
Install carbon monoxide alarms.
Dizzy or nauseous: get to fresh air, call {EMS}.

cards.w: Adult unresponsive and not breathing normally
s: Call {EMS} and send someone for an AED.
Push hard and fast in the center of the chest.
At least 2 in (5 cm) deep, 100 to 120 per minute.
Keep going until help or an AED arrives.
Heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone.
Other hand on top, fingers interlaced.
Arms straight, shoulders right over your hands.
Let the chest come all the way back up after each push.

cards.w: Only if you are trained and willing
s: After 30 compressions, give 2 breaths.
Tilt the head back and lift the chin.
Seal the mouth or use a mask, 1 second per breath.
Watch the chest rise, then resume compressions.

imgs.c: Scriptir , based on User:Rama 's work, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

cards.w: From age 1 to puberty, unresponsive, not breathing
s: Call {EMS} on speaker and start CPR.
One or two hands on the lower half of the breastbone.
Push about 2 in (5 cm) deep, 100 to 120 per minute.
30 compressions, then 2 breaths if trained.
Call {EMS} on speaker.
Two thumbs, or the heel of one hand, on the breastbone.
Push about 1.5 in (4 cm) deep, 100 to 120 per minute.
30 compressions, then 2 gentle breaths if trained.

cards.w: As soon as the defibrillator arrives
s: Turn it on and follow the voice prompts.
Bare the chest and stick the pads as pictured.
No one touches the person during analysis or shock.
Restart CPR right after the shock.
No response when you tap and shout.
Not breathing, or only gasping.
Call {EMS}, start CPR, get an AED.
Gasping is not normal breathing.

imgs.c: Rama, CC BY-SA 3.0 fr, Wikimedia Commons

cards.w: Do not wait to see if it passes
s: Chest pain or pressure, may spread to arm, jaw or back.
Short of breath, cold sweat, nausea.
Call {EMS} right away.
Chew one adult aspirin unless allergic or told not to.

cards.t: Child in cardiac arrest, you are alone
s: Give 2 minutes of CPR first.
Then leave briefly to call {EMS} and get an AED.
With a phone: call on speaker and start right away.
Come back and keep going until help arrives.
Use child pads or the child setting if available.
Otherwise, adult pads are fine.
Small chest: one pad on the front, one on the back.
Pads must not touch each other.

cards.t: Heart attack signs can differ in women
cards.w: Chest pain is not always the main sign
s: Shortness of breath, nausea or vomiting.
Pain in the back, jaw, neck or arms.
Unusual tiredness, cold sweat, lightheadedness.
Do not wait: call {EMS}.
Give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades.
Then 5 abdominal thrusts just above the navel.
Repeat until the object comes out.
If they collapse, call {EMS} and start CPR.

imgs.c: US ARMY MEDICAL DEPARTMENT CENTER AN…, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons
Evolution and evolvability, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

cards.w: After 5 back blows, if still choking
s: Stand behind, wrap your arms around the waist.
Fist just above the navel, thumb side in.
Grab the fist with your other hand.
Quick inward and upward thrusts, 5 times.

imgs.c: US ARMY MEDICAL DEPARTMENT CENTER AN…, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons
US ARMY MEDICAL DEPARTMENT CENTER AN…, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons
Evolution and evolvability, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

s: Face down along your forearm, head lower than chest.
5 back blows with the heel of your hand.
Turn face up: 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand.
Repeat. If unresponsive, call {EMS} and start CPR.

cards.w: When you cannot reach around the belly
s: Give 5 back blows first.
Arms under the armpits, hands on the lower breastbone.
Give 5 sharp chest thrusts backward.
Alternate until the object comes out.

imgs.c: US ARMY MEDICAL DEPARTMENT CENTER AN…, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

s: Ask: "Are you choking?"
If they can cough hard, let them keep coughing.
If they cannot cough, speak or breathe, act now.
Back blows, then abdominal thrusts.

imgs.c: US ARMY MEDICAL DEPARTMENT CENTER AN…, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

s: Call {EMS} if you can, even without speaking.
Fist above your navel, grab it with your other hand.
Thrust hard inward and upward.
Or push your belly hard against a chair back.
Near arm out at a right angle.
Far hand under the near cheek.
Bend the far knee and roll them toward you.
Tilt the head back, call {EMS}, keep checking breathing.

imgs.c: Rama, CC BY-SA 3.0 fr, Wikimedia Commons
Rama, CC BY-SA 3.0 fr, Wikimedia Commons

cards.w: An unconscious tongue can block breathing
s: One hand on the forehead, tilt the head back.
Two fingers under the chin, lift it.
Look, listen and feel for breathing.
Check for no more than 10 seconds.

imgs.c: Scriptir , based on User:Rama 's work, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons
Vassia Atanassova Vector: Offnfopt, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

s: Help them sit upright and stay calm.
Help them use their reliever inhaler, with a spacer.
Repeat as their action plan says.
Call {EMS} if no relief or they cannot speak.
Use their epinephrine auto-injector in the outer thigh.
Call {EMS}.
Let them sit up, or lie flat if faint.
No better in 5 to 15 minutes: a second dose may help.

imgs.c: Mikael Häggström , M.D., CC0, Wikimedia Commons

cards.w: Unresponsive, slow or no breathing, tiny pupils
s: Call {EMS}.
Give naloxone nasal spray into one nostril.
Not breathing normally: start CPR.
Stay with them; a second dose may be needed.
Remove the safety cap. Never put a thumb over the tip.
Press firmly into the outer thigh, through clothing if needed.
Hold as long as the device says, usually a few seconds.
Call {EMS}. Note the time of the dose.

imgs.c: Mikael Häggström , M.D., CC0, Wikimedia Commons

s: Lay them on their back, tilt the head back.
Nozzle in one nostril, press the plunger firmly.
Call {EMS}. Start CPR if not breathing normally.
No response in 2 to 3 minutes: second dose, other nostril.

cards.w: To check breathing or start CPR
s: Kneel beside them and straighten their arms.
Support the head and neck with one hand.
Roll the body toward you as one unit.
Keep the head in line with the body.
Call {EMS}. Wear gloves if you can.
Press hard directly on the wound with a cloth.
Do not lift the cloth; add more on top.
Keep pressing until help takes over.

cards.w: Life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg
s: Place it 2 to 3 in (5 to 7 cm) above the wound.
Never on a joint.
Tighten until the bleeding stops. It will hurt.
Note the time. Do not loosen it.

imgs.c: Bizhan Khodabandeh, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

cards.w: Once direct pressure has slowed the bleeding
s: Thick pad of gauze over the wound.
Wrap a bandage firmly around it.
Bleeding through? Add another layer on top.
Check fingers or toes stay warm and pink.
Sit up and lean forward, not back.
Pinch the soft part of the nose.
Hold firmly for at least 10 minutes.
Get care if it lasts more than 20 minutes.

cards.w: Finger, toe or limb cut off
s: Control the bleeding first. Call {EMS}.
Wrap the part in a clean, damp cloth.
Seal it in a plastic bag.
Put the bag on ice, never the part directly on ice.
Wash your hands.
Rinse the wound under clean running water.
Press with a clean cloth to stop bleeding.
Cover with a bandage. Watch for redness or pus.
Do not pull it out.
Press around it to control bleeding.
Pad around the object so it cannot move.
Call {EMS}.

cards.w: The most versatile item in a kit
s: Open flat: it makes a full sling.
Fold the point to the long edge.
Fold in half again for a wide cravat.
Fold once more for a narrow tie.

cards.t: Bandaging the head, ear or jaw
cards.w: Scalp and face wounds bleed a lot
s: Press a clean dressing on the wound.
Hold it with a cravat around the head.
Clear fluid from the ear after a fall: do not block it.
Call {EMS} for any serious head injury.

cards.w: Wounds that are hard to wrap
s: Dressing on the wound first.
Cravat over the shoulder, ends under the opposite armpit.
Tie it snugly but not tight.
Check the hand stays warm and pink.
Bend the joint slightly first.
Center a cravat over the dressing.
Cross the ends behind the joint and back over.
Tie off to the side, not over the wound.

cards.w: Cut on the palm or back of the hand
s: Dressing on the wound, padding in the palm.
Let the hand curl gently around it.
Wrap from the wrist over the hand and back.
Leave fingertips visible to check circulation.

cards.w: Cut on the sole or top of the foot
s: Dressing on the wound.
Cravat under the sole, ends crossed over the top.
Wrap around the ankle and tie in front.
Leave the toes visible to check them.
Dressing on the wound.
Wrap a cravat or roller bandage around it.
Each turn overlaps the last by half.
Firm but not tight. Check fingers or toes.

cards.w: Organs may show through the wound
s: Call {EMS}.
Lay them on their back, knees bent.
Do not push organs back in.
Cover with a moist, clean cloth. Nothing to eat or drink.

cards.w: Bleeding from the neck, armpit or groin
s: Call {EMS}.
Push gauze or clean cloth deep into the wound.
Keep packing until it is full.
Press hard with both hands, without stopping.
Cool under cool running water for at least 10 minutes.
Remove rings and tight items before swelling.
Cover loosely with clean plastic wrap.
No ice, butter or creams. Large burn: call {EMS}.

cards.w: Splash of cleaner, bleach or other chemical
s: Rinse right away with lots of lukewarm water.
Keep the eye open, rinse from the nose outward.
Continue for at least 15 minutes.
Then call {POISON} or {EMS}.
Keep the limb still, as you found it.
Do not try to straighten it.
Cold pack wrapped in cloth, up to 20 minutes.
Call {EMS} if bone shows or the limb is cold or blue.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

s: Support the arm across the chest.
Use a sling or a folded cloth tied behind the neck.
Do not force the arm into position.
Check that fingers stay warm and pink.

imgs.c: DataBase Center for Life Science (DB…, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
DataBase Center for Life Science (DB…, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

s: Rest the injured part.
Cold pack wrapped in cloth, 20 minutes at a time.
Raise it if that eases the pain.
See a doctor if you cannot bear weight.

cards.w: After a fall or a blow to the head
s: Keep them still; do not move the neck if unsure.
Cold pack on any bump.
Call {EMS} if confused, vomiting or drowsy.
Watch them closely for the next 24 hours.
Move them only if staying is more dangerous.
Drag by the clothes or on a blanket.
Pull along the length of the body.
Keep head and neck in line. Call {EMS}.

imgs.c: U.S. Navy, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons
U.S. Navy, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons
FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain
FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

cards.w: Fall from height, car crash, diving accident
s: Do not move them unless they are in danger.
Ask them to keep still.
Hold the head steady in the position found.
Call {EMS}. Breathing stops: start CPR.
Do not rub the eye.
Rinse with clean, lukewarm water.
Object stuck in the eye: do not remove it.
Cover the eye loosely and get medical care.
Pick it up by the crown, never the root.
If dirty, rinse briefly. Do not scrub.
Put it back in the socket, or keep it in milk or saliva.
See a dentist right away.
Wash with soap and running water for several minutes.
Press with a clean cloth to stop bleeding.
Cover with a clean bandage.
See a doctor: infection and rabies risk. Severe: {EMS}.

cards.w: Small piece of wood, glass or metal under the skin
s: Wash your hands and the area.
Clean tweezers, grip the end close to the skin.
Pull out at the same angle it went in.
Wash again and cover. Deep or in the eye: get care.
Leave it intact if you can.
Cover with a padded bandage.
If it breaks, wash it and keep the skin flap.
Redness, warmth or pus: see a doctor.

cards.w: Only if help is far away or you must move them
s: Splint the limb in the position you found it.
Pad the splint and extend it past the joints above and below.
Tie it on, knots on the splint side, not over the injury.
Check fingers or toes for warmth and feeling.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

cards.t: Check circulation after a splint or bandage
s: Compare fingers or toes with the other side.
Warm, pink and able to feel touch? Good.
Cold, pale, blue or numb: loosen it.
Recheck every 15 minutes.
Pin the shirt tail up over the injured arm.
Or loop a belt around the neck and the wrist.
Or fold the jacket flap up and fasten it.
Strips of cloth can tie the arm to the body.

cards.w: Pain and swelling between shoulder and elbow
s: Support the forearm in a sling.
Bind the arm against the chest with a wide band.
The chest becomes the splint.
Check the fingers. Get medical care.
Padded board, sticks or rolled magazine under the arm.
From the elbow to past the fingertips.
Tie above and below the injury.
Rest the arm in a sling, fingers slightly higher than the elbow.

cards.t: Splinting a lower leg or ankle
cards.w: Only if you must move them before help arrives
s: A pillow, rolled towel or blanket can be the splint.
Wrap it around the leg from knee to foot.
Tie at several points, not over the injury.
Check the toes for warmth and feeling.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain
FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

cards.w: Severe pain, leg may look short or turned out
s: Call {EMS}. Do not move them unless in danger.
Keep them still and warm.
Watch for shock: pale, cold, clammy skin.
Splint only if you must move them.
Keep the knee in the position found.
Pad around it to support it.
Cold pack wrapped in cloth, 20 minutes.
Cannot bear weight or knee looks deformed: get care.

cards.t: Splinting a leg to the other leg
cards.w: When nothing rigid is at hand
s: Put padding between the legs.
Gently bring the good leg next to the injured one.
Tie them together above and below the injury.
Never tie directly over the injury.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

cards.w: Pain at the front of the shoulder, arm held close
s: Support the arm in a sling.
Add a wide band around the arm and chest.
Do not push on the bump.
Get medical care.

cards.w: Shoulder looks out of place, arm cannot move
s: Do not try to pop it back in.
Support the arm in the position they find most comfortable.
Sling and a wide band around the chest.
Cold pack, then get medical care.

cards.w: Only to get someone away from danger
s: Light person: carry in your arms, under back and knees.
Pack-strap: their arms over your shoulders, hold their wrists.
Lift with your legs, keep your back straight.
Not for suspected neck or back injuries.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain
FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

cards.w: Moving someone out of danger with a helper
s: Rescuer 1 at the head: arms under theirs, grasp their wrists.
Rescuer 2 between the legs, holding under the knees.
Lift together on a count of three.
Walk in step, facing the same direction.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

cards.w: Down stairs or through narrow halls
s: Sit them in a sturdy chair without wheels.
Rescuer 1 tilts the chair back from behind.
Rescuer 2 lifts the front legs.
Go slowly. Not for neck or back injuries.

imgs.c: FEMA, CERT Basic Training (2019), Public domain

cards.w: Conscious person who can hold on
s: Each rescuer grips their own right wrist with the left hand.
Then grips the other rescuer's left wrist: a square seat.
The person sits and puts an arm around each rescuer.
Stand up together, walk in step.

cards.w: Weak or slightly injured but able to stand
s: Stand at their injured side.
Their arm over your shoulders, hold their wrist.
Your other arm around their waist.
Two helpers: one on each side. Go slowly.

cards.w: Two poles and a blanket or two jackets
s: Fold a blanket around two poles in thirds.
Or slide poles through the sleeves of two zipped jackets.
Test it with an uninjured person first.
At least two carriers, lift on command.

cards.t: Object in a child's nose or ear
s: Do not poke with tweezers or cotton swabs.
Nose: close the other nostril, blow gently.
Ear: tilt the head to that side and wait.
Still there: see a doctor. Trouble breathing: {EMS}.
Brush off any dry powder first.
Remove contaminated clothing and jewelry.
Flush with running water for 15 to 20 minutes.
Call {POISON}. Large area or pain: {EMS}.

cards.w: Swelling and bruising around the eye
s: Cold pack for 15 minutes, no pressure on the eye.
Keep the head raised.
Blurred or double vision, blood in the eye: urgent care.
Cannot move the eye or severe pain: {EMS}.

cards.w: After a blow to the face
s: Lean forward and pinch the soft part if it bleeds.
Cold pack, gently, for 15 minutes.
Crooked nose or cannot breathe through it: see a doctor.
Clear fluid from the nose or severe headache: {EMS}.

cards.w: Sharp pain when breathing or coughing
s: Help them sit upright.
Hold a pillow against the chest when they cough.
Do not wrap the chest tightly.
Short of breath or coughing blood: call {EMS}.
Face: does one side droop?
Arm: does one arm drift down?
Speech: slurred or strange?
Time: call {EMS} now and note the time.

imgs.c: United States Food and Drug Administ…, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

s: Clear the area and cushion the head.
Do not hold them down or put anything in the mouth.
Time it. Over 5 minutes: call {EMS}.
Afterward, place them in the recovery position.
Awake and able to swallow: give sugar.
Juice, regular soda or glucose tablets.
Recheck after 15 minutes; repeat if needed.
Unresponsive: call {EMS}, nothing by mouth.

cards.w: Feels faint or has just fainted
s: Help them lie down flat.
Raise the legs if there is no injury.
Loosen tight clothing, give fresh air.
Not breathing normally: call {EMS} and start CPR.
Call {POISON} for advice.
Unresponsive or not breathing: call {EMS}.
Do not make them vomit.
Keep the container to show what was taken.

cards.w: Pale, cold, clammy skin, fast breathing, weak
s: Call {EMS}.
Help them lie flat on their back.
Keep them warm with a blanket.
Nothing to eat or drink. Stay with them.

cards.w: Fast breathing, racing heart, sense of dread
s: Stay calm and move to a quiet place.
Breathe slowly with them: in for 4, out for 6.
Reassure them that it will pass.
Chest pain, first episode or doubt: call {EMS}.

cards.w: Confused, vomiting, slow breathing, hard to wake
s: Call {EMS}. Do not let them sleep it off.
Unresponsive but breathing: recovery position.
Stay with them; watch their breathing.
No coffee or cold showers. Not breathing: CPR.

cards.t: Seizure with fever in a child
s: Lay the child on a safe surface, on their side.
Nothing in the mouth. Do not hold them down.
Time it. Over 5 minutes or trouble breathing: call {EMS}.
Afterward, have a doctor check the child.
Fever is 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher.
Call the doctor right away, even at night.
Floppy, hard to wake or breathing hard: call {EMS}.
Do not give medicine unless the doctor says so.
Signs: dry mouth, no tears, few wet diapers, sleepy.
Give small, frequent sips of oral rehydration solution.
Keep breastfeeding babies.
Very sleepy, sunken eyes or no urine for 8 hours: get care.

cards.w: Can burn through tissue within hours
s: Call {POISON} or {EMS} right away.
Go to the emergency room even without symptoms.
Do not make the child vomit.
Poison control may advise honey for children over 1.
Confusion, fast heartbeat, fast breathing.
Fever, shivering or feeling very cold.
Extreme pain, clammy or mottled skin.
These signs with an infection: call {EMS} and ask about sepsis.

cards.w: Hot skin, confusion, may stop sweating
s: Call {EMS}. This is life-threatening.
Cool fast: cold water immersion up to the neck.
Or soak with water and fan hard.
Move to shade, remove extra clothing.
Move to a cool place, loosen clothing.
Cool wet cloths on the skin.
Sip cool water or a sports drink.
Vomiting or getting worse: call {EMS}.
Get them out of the cold and wind.
Replace wet clothes with dry ones.
Wrap in blankets, cover the head.
Warm sweet drink if fully alert. Severe: call {EMS}.

cards.w: Contact with a live wire or appliance
s: Do not touch them until the power is off.
Unplug or cut power at the breaker.
Call {EMS}.
Check breathing; start CPR if needed.

imgs.c: Gregors, Copyrighted free use, Wikimedia Commons

cards.w: Person in trouble in the water
s: Reach or throw something; do not go in unless trained.
Call {EMS}.
Out of the water and not breathing: start CPR.
Give rescue breaths with compressions if trained.
Fine-tipped tweezers, as close to the skin as you can.
Pull straight up with steady pressure.
Clean the bite and your hands.
Rash or fever in the next weeks: see a doctor.
Remove the stinger quickly.
Wash with soap and water.
Cold pack for 10 minutes to ease swelling.
Trouble breathing or face swelling: call {EMS}.
Call {EMS}. Move away from the snake.
Keep the person calm and still.
Remove rings and tight items near the bite.
No tourniquet, cutting, suction or ice.

cards.w: Burning pain, red lines on the skin
s: Get out of the water.
Rinse with vinegar for at least 30 seconds.
Then soak in water as hot as is comfortable, about 20 minutes.
Trouble breathing or chest pain: call {EMS}.

cards.w: Numb, white or grayish, hard skin
s: Get to a warm place. Do not rub the skin.
Do not rewarm if it could freeze again.
Soak in warm water, 99 to 104 °F, for 20 to 30 minutes.
Get medical care. Treat hypothermia first.
They carry no electric charge: it is safe to touch.
Move to a safer place if the storm continues.
Call {EMS}.
Not breathing normally: start CPR right away.

cards.w: Headache, dizziness, nausea, several people sick
s: Get everyone into fresh air.
Do not go back inside.
Call {EMS}.
Not breathing normally: start CPR.

cards.w: Painful muscle spasms after effort in the heat
s: Stop and rest in a cool place.
Sip a sports drink or water.
Gently stretch the muscle.
Wait for the cramps to go before resuming.
Get out of the sun.
Cool showers or damp cloths.
Drink extra water. Moisturize gently.
Do not pop blisters. Large blisters or fever: see a doctor.

cards.w: Most bites happen when people handle snakes
s: Triangular head, heat pits between eyes and nostrils.
Leave it alone; back away slowly.
Never try to catch or kill it.
If bitten: stay still and call {EMS}.

cards.w: Red, yellow and black bands, southern US
s: Shy, rarely bites unless handled.
Symptoms can be delayed for hours.
Any bite: call {EMS}, even without pain.
Keep the person calm and still.

cards.w: Black widow or brown recluse suspected
s: Wash with soap and water.
Cold pack wrapped in cloth, 10 minutes on and off.
Call {POISON} for advice.
Severe pain, cramps or trouble breathing: call {EMS}.
Wash the area and apply a cold pack.
Keep the stung limb still and at heart level.
Call {POISON} for advice.
Child stung, twitching or trouble breathing: call {EMS}.

cards.w: Leaves of three, let it be
s: Wash skin with soap and cool water as soon as you can.
Wash clothes, tools and pet fur that touched the plant.
Do not scratch; cool compresses ease the itch.
Rash on face or eyes, or trouble breathing: get care.
Black widow: shiny black, red hourglass under the belly.
Brown recluse: brown, violin shape on the back.
Shake out shoes, gloves and bedding in storage areas.
Bitten: wash, cold pack, call {POISON}.

cards.w: Headache, nausea, dizziness at high altitude
s: Stop going higher. Rest.
Drink fluids, avoid alcohol.
Not better or getting worse: go down.
Confusion, clumsy walking or breathless at rest: {EMS}, descend.

cards.w: Know what is normal for you
s: In a mirror: arms down, then raised. Look for changes.
